messages.subject: GBM design document
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am interested in contributing to this project and wondering if there is a high-level document that describes how GBM works under the hood. Also, which is the best branch to start form? Someone with the user name JHickey has forked the repo and made quite a lot of changes. I'm wondering if that is where I should start or if those changes are independent from the core GBM developers.

Thanks

-Eric

messages.subject: Re: GBM design document
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

James Hickey's changes will be the future of GBM. He's being funded by AstraZeneca[0], who use GBM for mining clinical trial data, to refactor the code to improve extensibility and maintainability.  When the work is finished and we're confident it's correct - and you've seen it's quite extensive - it'll be merged back in. We're also going to add in Terry Therneau's Cox code, which will considerably improve gbm's time to event facilities.

The work lives at

https://github.com/scientific-computing-solutions/gbm

I've held off from merging it into gbm-developers/gbm/master so far because I'd like to get a coherent worthwhile fully tested change that we know works. Any comments on the code are welcome!

There will be a design document produced as part of this, but we don't yet have it.

Hope this helps,

pdm

messages.subject_clean: here's where we're up to with the refactoring
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Here's where we've got to:

We've been simplifying the structure of the decision tree growing and again applying appropriate design patterns and class design.  This has been quite a lot of work and it's not quite finished yet.

We're going to continue with that, begin testing gbm under UBSAN so that we can be as sure as we can be that we aren't triggering undefined behaviour, and introduce unit tests for the tree growing code.  After we've done that, the next step is to replace the coxph code with that provided by Terry T.

Any feedback or suggestions are welcome, and progress may be viewed at

https://github.com/scientific-computing-solutions/gbm

Best wishes,

--
pdm

messages.subject: more updates
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

We've finished our fourth sprint of work on GBM.  We have finished simplifying the decision tree growing code and finished off applying appropriate design patterns.  We also did a bit of work running GBM with UBSAN compiler flags enabled and finding and fixing the errors that produced.

The tree growing algorithm is now more readily parallelisable via OpenMP and has modified the searching so that better splits are identified when growing a tree.  These changes mean that results may change slightly from before and the algorithm is more computationally intensive, and hence slower.  A future sprint will be aimed at optimization.

We are now - in sprint 5 - updating the Cox proportional hazards distribution with code provided by Terry Therneau, which should fix our Cox bugs and also add in quite a bit of additional functionality.

After this we're planning on updating the R front-end in sprint 6, in preparation for documentation, testing and optimization to follow.

Again, complaints, comments, and suggestions are very welcome!

--
pdm

messages.subject: survival update
messages.body_plain:
I've attached an update of the survival routines.
Summary: No change in input or output, some lines removed from mresid2.c.

Long form: I've just released survival2.39 to CRAN, and as part of that update I carefully
worked through several nasty data sets from users, that had given numerical issue in the
likelilhood kernel of coxph.  I now understand the issues more thoroughly.  In select
cases, certain additions and subtractions need to be done in just the right order so as to
avoid cancellation.  The lines removed from mresid2.c guard against a case that, I now
realize, does not happen due to the other changes that had been made.

Terry T.

messages.subject: Re: survival update
messages.body_plain:
Paul,
  The other part of the equation is that all of these edge cases happen due to large values for eta= linear predictor.  (The denominator for all the totals in coxph is sum( exp(eta[i])), summed over those currently at risk.)   I don't think that gbm will ever produce such values.  All the cases I've seen to date involved a very badly skewed but statistically significant variable, so that X \beta was huge for the subject(s) way out in the right hand tail.  I pointed out to the source of the most recent problem data set that they should perhaps question their linearity assumption, since the MLE solution then implied a relative risk of approx 10^40 for one observation, which is greater than the number of atoms in the earth.

The gbm variant does not need to be nearly as "on guard" against these edge cases, it suffices to do things sensibly.

There is one other thing to be aware of, though I don't think it is an issue for gbm.  The first derivative is mX where m is the martingale residual.  Since sum(m) =0, adding a large constant to one of the columns of X leaves the answer unchanged: unless that constant is outrageous.  Adding 10^15 to a 0/1 column would for instance put one at the edge of precision.  So will a term of "x * group" in a coxph model where x is a POSIXct time value and group is 0/1. (Yes I've had such a bug report; it wasn't POSIXct but something very similar in terms of mean vs std).  But again, people don't tend to put interaction terms into a gbm equation.  You shouldn't have to standardize X.

Terry T.
